summary.text: The Continental Army was founded on June 14, 1775 by the Second Continental Congress to coordinate the colonies' defense against Britain in the Revolutionary War.
George Washington served as its commander-in-chief, and state troops and volunteer militia periodically supplemented it.
Congress disbanded it on June 2, 1784, apart from a few small detachments, and the United States Army succeeded it.

facts.label: Commander
facts.value: George Washington, who took no pay beyond expenses

facts.label: First enlistments
facts.value: One year, for the first ten companies

facts.label: Later enlistments
facts.value: Three years or the length of the war

items.prompt: In early 1775 the colonies had no national army. What had each colony relied on for defense before then?

options.label: A permanent army paid for by the British Parliament
Regiments of mercenaries hired from foreign nations
Part-time citizen-soldiers in local militias, or temporary provincial troops
Full-time soldiers trained by a central colonial council

items.explain: Colonies relied on militias of part-time citizen-soldiers or raised temporary provincial troops, as in the French and Indian War.

items.prompt: The 1776 army nearly collapsed when soldiers' one-year terms ran out. How did Congress try to prevent that crisis later?

options.label: It extended enlistment to three years or the length of the war
It doubled the pay of every soldier who stayed on
It replaced volunteers with soldiers hired from overseas
It allowed soldiers to return home each winter

items.explain: Longer enlistment terms were meant to avoid the year-end crises that drained the army, including the near-collapse at the end of 1776.

items.prompt: Some Americans disliked having a standing army, yet Congress created one. Why?

options.label: Local militias had refused to take part in the fighting at all
Britain had demanded a national army before it would negotiate
Washington insisted on an army before he would accept a post
The war against Britain seemed to need the discipline and organization of a central military

items.explain: Despite the aversion to standing armies, the war was seen as requiring the discipline and organization of a central military.

items.prompt: How was Washington paid for serving as commander-in-chief throughout the war?

options.label: He received a fixed yearly salary set by Congress
He took no compensation except reimbursement of his expenses
He was given a share of captured British supplies
He was paid with grants of western land

items.explain: Washington served without any compensation except reimbursement of expenses.

items.prompt: In 1781–1782 Congress was bankrupt and voted to cut funding for the army. What did Washington have to deal with?

options.label: A British invasion of Philadelphia, which he turned back
A rebellion in Congress, which he helped to end
Mutinies in the Pennsylvania and New Jersey lines, which he put down
A mass desertion to the French army, which he stopped

items.explain: With the army short of money and popular support at an all-time low, Washington had to put down mutinies in the Pennsylvania and New Jersey lines.

items.prompt: Members of Congress on the first five-person committee overseeing the army were too busy to run it. What did Congress do?

options.label: It formed a new Board of War made up of commissioners who were not members of Congress
It gave Washington sole control over every army decision
It handed the army's management over to each state
It put the army under a single member of Congress

items.explain: Because the committee's members were busy with Congress, a new Board of War was formed from commissioners who were not members of Congress.

paragraphs.heading: An army built from scratch
paragraphs.text: When the Revolutionary War opened at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775, the rebelling colonists had no standing army to call on. Until then each colony had leaned on its militia, a body of part-time citizen-soldiers who guarded their own area. In wartime a colony might also raise provincial troops for a limited stretch, as happened in the French and Indian War. As trouble with Britain grew, colonists began reorganizing their militias, and training stepped up after the Intolerable Acts of 1774.

paragraphs.heading: Founding in 1775
paragraphs.text: Richard Henry Lee had suggested a national militia, but the First Continental Congress turned the idea down. On June 14, 1775, the Second Continental Congress, sitting in Philadelphia, voted to create the Continental Army for the shared defense of the colonies against Britain. It took in the New England Army of Observation already camped outside Boston and the forces around New York City. The same day, Congress unanimously chose George Washington as Commander in Chief.

paragraphs.heading: Washington in command
paragraphs.text: Washington accepted, went straight to Boston, and led a siege of the city that succeeded. He stayed in command for the whole war and took no pay, only repayment of his expenses. The army drew its soldiers from the colonies and, after 1776, from the United States. State troops and volunteer militia filled out its ranks from time to time.

paragraphs.heading: Debate and reform
paragraphs.text: Some Americans disliked the idea of a standing army on principle. Yet the war seemed to demand the discipline and organization of a central military. So the army kept changing, reorganizing its units again and again, and in the end it won support from France, which wanted to push back British influence in North America. Military business was first handled by the whole Congress, then by a standing Board of War and Ordnance set up in June 1776.

paragraphs.heading: Fixing the enlistment problem
paragraphs.text: The first troops enlisted for just one year, so the army faced a crisis each time a year closed and terms ran out. At the end of 1776 it nearly collapsed this way, which could have lost the war by simple default. Congress passed the Eighty-eight Battalion Resolve, which ordered each state to supply regiments in proportion to its population. To avoid those year-end crises, enlistments were stretched to three years or for as long as the war lasted.

paragraphs.heading: The hardest years
paragraphs.text: The years 1781 and 1782 brought the gravest crisis on the American side. Congress had run out of money, so it struggled to replace soldiers whose three-year terms had ended. Public backing for the war fell to its lowest point, and Washington had to put down mutinies in the Pennsylvania Line and the New Jersey Line. Even with its funding cut, the army under Washington still won important strategic victories.

paragraphs.heading: Disbanding and legacy
paragraphs.text: Once peace with Britain returned, most regiments were sent home in an orderly way. Congress disbanded the army on June 2, 1784, keeping only small groups of privates at Fort Pitt, West Point and other military storehouses, plus a small artillery unit. The force that followed it was the United States Army, which still exists today.
